items.title: Water dissolves more things than any other liquid
items.claim: Water is called 'the universal solvent'. It dissolves more substances than any other liquid — salts, sugars, gases, many organic molecules. Yet it has only three atoms and a simple structure.
items.prompt: What makes water such a versatile solvent?

options.text: Water is highly polar (large dipole), forms hydrogen bonds with H-bond donors and acceptors, and has a high dielectric constant (around 80) that weakens ionic attractions enough for ions to separate and become solvated
Water is the only liquid on Earth that occurs naturally

items.reveal:
Water's bent shape and large O-H bond polarity give a permanent dipole moment of 1.85 debye. Each water molecule can form up to 4 hydrogen bonds — two as donor, two as acceptor.

Water's dielectric constant of about 80 (vs about 2 for hexane) means it screens ionic charges strongly: a cation and anion that would attract each other electrostatically in vacuum are 80 times less attracted in water, so they separate.

Non-polar substances (oils, wax) lack matching interactions and so won't dissolve. 'Universal' is overstating things — water is just a brilliant solvent for polar and ionic species, and we mostly care about polar and ionic species.
items.why: Water is treated as a passive background. Its chemistry actively shapes whether ions stay dissolved or precipitate.

items.title: A blacksmith's anvil works because of heat capacity, not strength
items.claim: A 100 kg steel anvil sits cold under a 1300°C glowing iron bar. The bar bends; the anvil doesn't even warm to the touch. The mass of the anvil sets the rate at which the bar cools — but each strike still leaves the anvil cool.
items.prompt: Why doesn't the heat 'flow' into the anvil and damage it?

options.text: Heat flow is finite over the brief contact time; the anvil's large heat capacity buffers any small heat input it does receive, keeping its temperature change tiny

items.reveal_title: Mass times specific heat = thermal inertia
items.reveal:
A 1 kg piece of red-hot iron at 1300°C contains about 580 kJ above ambient. Strike it once on a 100 kg anvil and transfer (very roughly) a few percent of that heat by contact. The anvil — 100 kg with specific heat 460 J/kg·K — warms by maybe 0.2°C.

Multiple strikes can heat parts of the anvil noticeably but it dissipates fast through the anvil's mass and into the ground via its sturdy base. Anvils last decades of professional use without damage.

The principle generalises: heat sinks on CPUs, heat reservoirs in steam plants, and the oceans' role as Earth's thermal flywheel all rely on the same mass-times-heat-capacity logic.
items.why: Heat is taught with single-substance examples. Real heat transfer is set by mass, specific heat, contact area and time — not just temperature difference.
